speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am now in a position to make a statement about the results of the 1953-54 wheat pool. This pool was closed as at April 29. I had suggested an earlier date but in the opinion of the Canadian wheat board a more satisfactory accounting could be made if the closing of the pool were delayed until after the opening of navigation on the great lakes and on the St. Lawrence. Therefore, the government agreed to the closing date recommended by the wheat board, namely, April 29, 1955.
From the standpoint of a marketing operation, the 1953-54 pool was the most difficult in the post-war history of the wheat board.
In the first place, as hon. members will recall, the 1953 wheat crop was the third in a succession of three bumper crops produced in the prairie provinces. In spite of a very high level of exports and domestic demand in
1951-52 and 1952-53, substantial stocks of wheat remained in elevators on July 31, 1953. Sales from the 1953-54 pool could not begin until these carryover stocks from the previous pool had been reduced to reasonable proportions. Actually, sales from the 1953-54 pool did not begin until February 1, 1954. To put the matter briefly, stocks of wheat were carried in the 1953-54 pool from August 1, 1953 to April 29, 1955-a period of 21 months. Sales operations were carried on over a period of 15 months. It is not surprising, therefore, that carrying charges applicable to the 1953-54 pool were substantially higher than in any previous pooling period administered by the wheat board.
Now, let me describe briefly the marketing situation faced by the wheat board during the life of the pool. Following the unprecedented export demand for cereals in
1952-53, world demand for wheat fell away sharply in the crop year 1953-54. As the house knows, our exports of wheat and flour in that crop year were 255 million bushels as compared with 385 million bushels in the preceding crop year. This decline in world demand affected particularly Canada, the United States and Australia.
While world demand improved during the first nine months of the present crop year, competition has been extremely keen and during this period the United States surplus disposal program has emerged as one of the chief factors in the international wheat position. Canadian export sales have improved, but not to the extent that would achieve the rapid movement of wheat hoped for earlier in the crop year.
The United States has a triple-barrelled surplus disposal program in effect. Wheat may be bartered for strategic materials, may be distributed to importing countries for local currencies which are usually left in the recipient country for development or other purposes, or may be given away as a relief measure. So far the cost of procurement of wheat in the United States for surplus disposal abroad has amounted to over $200 million. In addition to this surplus disposal program, which cannot be regarded in any way as ordinary commercial transactions, the United States have during the present crop year increased their export subsidies in order to effect sales. As at the end of March, the United States had increased their exports of wheat and flour by over 60 million bushels as compared with the previous crop year, and the increase will undoubtedly be larger by the end of the crop year.
The wheat board and the government expect, and are fully prepared, to deal with competition in world wheat markets. The record shows that we have met this competition most effectively. Canada has retained a high proportion of commercial markets throughout the world. In recent months, however, the surplus disposal programs of the United States are being pressed to the point where, in our opinion, they are having a disturbing effect upon commercial markets.
3782	HOUSE OF
1953-54 Wheat Pool Operations
The purpose behind the surplus disposal efforts of the United States is to increase consumption in areas that cannot afford to buy wheat. Canada has no quarrel with that principle. It is doubtful, however, whether anything is gained, and certainly much is lost, if surplus disposal programs are pushed to the point where they disturb normal trading relationships.
I should add that during the period of the 1953-54 pool, wheat prices declined substantially and this, of course, has lowered the return which the wheat board have been able to secure from their sales. With these general observations in mind, let me deal now with the financial results of the 1953-54 wheat pool.
Producers' deliveries of wheat to the pool were 398 million bushels. A total of 148-7 million bushels, including 21-4 million bushels of priced open sales contracts, were transferred to the 1953-54 pool from the 1952-53 pool as at January 30, 1954. Deliveries from others than producers were 1-4 million bushels, bringing the total volume of wheat in the pool to 548-1 million bushels. Completed sales to the close of business on April 29 amounted to 384 million bushels. Therefore there remained as at April 29 a balance of 164-1 million bushels. These stocks included 42-9 million bushels covered by priced open sales contracts and unsold stocks of 121 - 2 million bushels.
In closing out the 1953-54 pool the open sales contracts were transferred to the 1954-55 pool at contract prices and unsold stocks were transferred on the basis of board selling prices for April 29 less an allowance for carrying charges subsequent to the date of transfer and an allowance for market risk in the case of certain slow-moving grades.
The final operating surplus in the pool is $64,725,147.55 from which must be deducted the 10 cents per bushel interim payment made last fall. This payment amounted to $38,638,704.15. After providing for P.F.A.A. levy on the interim and final payments and after allowing for final payment expenses, the surplus for distribution to producers as a final payment is $25,411,407.89.
On producers' deliveries of 398 million bushels the average final payment is 6-384 cents per bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since my hon. friend spoke to me about the last part of his question this morning I have had an opportunity of seeing what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said about this aspect of the question and what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said in this house on April 1. I am afraid that at the present time there is nothing useful that can be added to what has been said already, both by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the Prime Minister. The matter which my hon. friend raises is now being noted and will be followed through by the officials of the department and brought to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he returns from Europe some time this week.
With regard to the first part of the question, as my hon. friend and other members know, there have been important developments during the past week. The German federal republic has entered NATO and into the full political and defence association with the western nations which we have hoped to

achieve for so long. A state treaty for Austria has been signed and 10 years of occupation ended. The leading western powers have invited the Soviet union to a meeting, both of heads of governments and of foreign ministers, and the Soviet union has accepted the invitation.
The Soviet union has tabled a series of proposals at the disarmament talks in London which contain significant changes of policy on some points relating to disarmament and which may point to some of the subjects to be discussed at a four power meeting. At a conference in Warsaw, the Soviet union has set up a unified command for its forces and the forces of its satellites in eastern Europe. We learn that Marshal Bulganin and Mr. Khrushchev will visit Yugoslavia.
So we may ask, what do all these rapid developments imply so far as relaxation of tension and a European and even world settlement are concerned? So far as the western nations are concerned, the various steps in their policies have been intended to lead eventually to peaceful negotiation of outstanding differences between east and west to remove the risk of world war. The invitation extended to the Soviet union to participate in discussions both between heads of governments and foreign ministers establishes this intention on the part of the western powers. It underlines the fervent desire of western nations to find any possible way of arriving at a peaceful settlement of outstanding issues based on recognition of the legitimate security interests and national freedom of the nations most directly concerned.
We may well ask, what are the Soviet intentions? The final signing of the Austrian state treaty and the apparent concessions on disarmament do lead one to hope for a greater willingness to discuss other problems. The extent of Soviet diplomatic activity does suggest that various far-reaching changes may be planned.
The Canadian government naturally welcomes the fact that high level talks between the leading western powers and the Soviet union will take place. We think that considerable progress can be made at these talks and that there are compelling reasons of national interest on both sides for representatives of these nations to examine the fundamental differences between them in the immediate future. We have noted the expressed desires of some Soviet leaders to negotiate with the west in spite of the basic ideological differences. We have noted the concessions made on specific points. We hope that the Soviet government will continue to respond to the deep desire of people in all countries for peaceful solutions of international problems.

Minister of Agriculture, or rather the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is sometimes difficult to know which department looks after which, with the distribution of marketing as between these two departments.
It has never been anywhere else but there.

It is a statement that will be received with deep regret on the part of the farming population generally that depends for its livelihood upon the marketing of wheat. Indeed, by the action of this government, on the basis of purchasing power during the period 1935 to 1939, farmers will be receiving on the farm a price of about 58 cents a bushel. When agriculture is not prosperous the Canadian people cannot be prosperous, for one-seventh of the population is directly dependent on agriculture and a further large segment of our population engaged in industry, transportation, etc., is directly affected. It has been estimated that farmers purchase for the average family four times more than does the urban family. I know that there will be a profound sense of disappointment on the part of western farmers when they are advised that the amount that they are to receive in the cutoff of the pool will be slightly over 6 cents a bushel. What is happening follows in consequence of what we of the opposition had

Wheat
warned against for several years-loss of markets arising through the failure of this government to act, when the portents and indications demanded effective action.
The wheat producer is receiving a disappointing final payment, one of the reasons being that failure to act. Since 1950 we of the opposition have been endeavouring to interest the government in the convening of a British commonwealth trade conference. The answer on every occasion has been that such a course was unnecessary. In the 1953 election the optimistic ministers of the government contended that there was nothing to be concerned about regarding the loss of markets and that Canada had so many markets she could scarcely produce enough to meet their demands.
We find ourselves now in a position dangerous to the economy of this country. The minister's attitude today was far removed from that ultra-optimism he exuded in the past. Today his attitude was one of realism based on experience. The failure to take the initiative during the last several years, based upon danger signals which indicated the threat and the peril to the Canadian wheat farmer directly and indirectly to the people of Canada, is now bringing its reward. I asked the minister how much were the carrying charges on the wheat in storage last year, and he said that was a question for the order paper. It is extremely hard to get answers to that question, Mr. Speaker. For a considerable length of time we have tried to ascertain what those carrying charges are. If I took him down correctly, the minister said that the increase in the carrying charges in the last year now being wound up was 8J cents per bushel. What those carrying charges are, we do not know. Three or four years ago they amounted to $17 million a year.
Two years or two and one-half years ago my recollection is that, on the basis of computation although not on information received from the responsible minister or the department, they amounted to some $25 million. That is a tremendous amount. On the basis of information that one is able to secure, I believe it is safe to say that the Canadian farmer in the last year has had taken from him in storage charges the amount of at least $65,000 a day. Whether or not those figures be correct, I do not know; but the amount has been tremendous and there are still in the elevators of this country large quantities of wheat which, to all intents and purposes, may be unmarketable. For the last year or so members on this side of the house have been endeavouring to get the minister to place before the house and the country a picture of the so-called aggressive policy for

the marketing of the farmers' wheat, but we have not been able to secure any information.
On May 12 the Canadian Press reported the situation. It is one dangerous in its import, one that challenges the Canadian economy. The report reads:
Canada's share of an expanding world wheat market has declined while that of the United States has increased. Thus the United States has recaptured the lead from Canada as the world's top exporter.
That is all within the last few years. What is this government's policy? You cannot blame the wheat board because the wheat board acts under the express direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the ministers of this government. What is that policy? What has been done? What active measures are being taken? My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia asked this afternoon and he received the usual illusory, uncertain, indefinite answer which indicated that the question might be answered in a general way by saying that no one need concern himself; for after all, this government knows best and things will turn out all right in the end. The Canadian Press report continues:
In the first eight months of the current crop year which began last August, total exports from the four major shippers-Canada, the U.S., Australia and Argentina-increased by 102,700,000 bushels to 517,500,000 from 414,800,000 a year ago, the bureau of statistics reported today.
Canada's shipments increased by 1,800,000 bushels out of an increase of 102,700,000 bushels during the course of the year. What of this government, that should have acted to provide markets for Canadian wheat, particularly when it enjoys a reputation for being the best wheat in the world? The report goes on to say this:
However, Canada's shipments increased only by 1,800,000 bushels to 172,700,000-
[DOT]-while those of the U.S. jumped by 64,200,000 to 189,900,000. The U.S. has led the world in wheat exports in most post-war years but in the first eight months of last year was far behind Canada-
The United States is trying to find markets. The Canadian government is hoping to find markets.

My right hon. friend makes an interruption but he did not answer the question today as to what the government is doing. The farmers of Canada want to know that.
This year the United States has been putting on a big export drive . . .
I ask the minister to tell the people of this country what kind of drive the wheat board and this government have been putting on.
None.

If it has been a drive, it has been a pedestrian one. Then the report goes on to mention that the United States has been giving some wheat away. I have asked the minister several times during the last year the question whether the United States was undermining the wheat market of the world by such action. I think in every case- and I have the quotations available-the minister's attitude was that there was nothing to worry about with regard to United States give-away policy, that it was of no serious importance. The United States has been selling seme of its wheat under defence and local currency deals. As far as defence deals are concerned, I realize that Canada cannot participate. But I ask the minister to tell the people of Canada why something cannot be done to provide for the exchange of our wheat by local currency deals such as those that are being made by the United States. What is the reason? Certainly the results revealed today indicate a lamentable failure on the part of this government to preserve our markets and to assure to Canadian farmers engaged in the production of wheat their fair and proper share of the world market.
More than that I will not say at this time for there is not available to members of this house information which permits of an extended analysis of the course being followed. On May 5 I asked this question:
How many bushels of wheat were in elevator and terminal storage in Canada as of the 30th July 1954?
That was not a difficult question to answer. That information is available. But parliament waits at the convenience of the department. The next question was:
What was the total amount paid for elevator and terminal storage for all wheat in storage between the 1st July, 1953 and the 30th July, 1954?
We wait for that information now embalmed in the form of an order for return passed today.
The next question had to do with terminal elevators being rented to private companies. I have no objection to some delay in that connection. But as far as the others are concerned the minister has the answers, or he would not have been able to report that carrying charges increased last year by 8J cents per bushel.
Mr. Speaker, what has happened in the last two or three years in the marketing of Canadian wheat indicates that this government has lost its way and that Canada's share of the world market, proportionately to that of other exporting countries, has been frittered away not only by the failure of this government to

act but by its refusal to admit that the problem even existed. Whenever the matter was raised in the house the government has answered in an offhand attitude of bravado, "After all, time will tell" or in effect saying, "All is well".
Today's revelation makes this a black Monday in the history of the wheat farmers of Canada. No one expects the government to do everything, but surely in the face of a world situation such as has prevailed in the last two or three years we should have had some action of an effective nature, something of an intensive sales campaign by the Department of Trade and Commerce, in place of optimistic statements made from time to time.
Having said that, sir, what I intend to refer to today is in general the development of our resources in order not only to meet the present unemployment situation but also to provide for development so as to assure all parts of Canada something approaching equality in national development to the end that our provinces may advance together reasonably equal in the opportunities that are afforded. speechtext: The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) will understand that I did not make a ruling. I said we have already done too much talking about the South Saskatchewan dam. All we have had from the government opposite is talk and more talk; promise and repromise. Now, after 20 years of successive and continuous promises to the people of Saskatchewan that something would be done, we get from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) of this country a continuing and definite "no". What is the Prime Minister's answer? It is the most amazing answer that anyone could possibly imagine. He says he cannot be convinced that it is in the national interest. How does one find out whether or not something is in the national interest? Surely the opinions of members of parliament should have some bearing on any conclusion as to whether or not this project is in the national interest. And, because of this, the Conservative and the Social Credit parties have supported the South Saskatchewan project.
Oh, the Liberal party has supported it, too-that is, some remnants of the Liberal party, some splinter members of the Liberal party and of the cabinet. of making political speeches. I am afraid if we wait for the Liberal party to build the South Saskatchewan dam, and if we wait for the present Prime Minister to build the South Saskatchewan dam, then, at the rate they are going, the dam will never be built. No, it will never be built because apparently the Prime Minister has a very narrow idea of what is in the national interest. His idea is so narrow, when considering what is in the national interest, that the farther a project gets away from Ottawa apparently, in his view, the less importance it has.

There is another reason why this dam should be built. Saskatchewan is short of electrical energy. Experts tell us that the building of the South Saskatchewan dam would provide 400 million kilowatt hours of electricity a year, a huge amount of electricity. This is something the people of Saskatchewan need as quickly as they can get it, not just for those years in which there might be bad crops but for each and every year of the years that lie ahead.
For all of these reasons I expect that opposition members will give unanimous support to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I hope that some of our western Liberal members of parliament, in particular Saskatchewan Liberal members, will stand by the interests of the people who sent them here and support this reasonable and worth-while amendment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the appeal which has been made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), in view of the fact that I am a member from Saskatchewan, I feel I should say a few words at this stage. The South Saskatchewan river dam was not known as such to any person either inside or outside this house until 1946, which is not 20 years ago. The Minister of Agriculture was responsible for trying to find a place where the dam could be built and this had to be done before talking about building a dam. No one else in this house was responsible for those activities; the responsibility was that of the Department of Agriculture and it was assumed by the Department of Agriculture.
Under its activities in connection with the P.F.R.A. it endeavoured to find out whether there was some place on the South Saskatchewan where a dam could be built, if it could be built, and just what the effects would be. That was found out by 1946 and since 1946 we have been discussing the possibility of building it. At no time have I taken any other position than that it should be built. I have not said it is going to be built. I think every hon. member on all sides of the house will agree with that. I have constantly advocated the building of the dam and I still advocate the building of the dam.

. As I said a few moments ago when interrupting, I am still convinced that some time the government of Canada is going to build the South Saskatchewan river dam and I expect that the government of Canada that does build it will be a Liberal government. I have no hesitation in saying that.

In times like these, in days when there are nothing but floods in a country, I think it is hard to appreciate how important irrigation can be. Many people out there say, "Let us get the water out of the country and never talk about it again". I understand how the people feel down in the Qu'Appelle country and in the other areas recently flooded by the terrible storms in Saskatchewan. South Saskatchewan River Project It is the same with water. But in the cycles of drought that occur in the western country there comes a time when irrigation water is just like lifeblood. I am sure the time will come when the people of Saskatchewan will want that water badly. I think that the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) wanted to say something about the serious decline in farm income and perhaps to use that fact as one of his arguments for the building of this dam. During the past several weeks, in the course of the budget debate and others, a number of things have been said about the serious decline in farm cash income. My colleague the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) the other day, I think, mentioned the fact that since 1951 there has been a decline of $1,025 million or some such figure in the net income of the farmers of this country. That is an extremely serious decline in farm income.
I understand that in this past year farm income made up only about 6 per cent of the total national income, although the farmers as a class make up about 16 per cent of the total population of Canada. That is far below the fair share of farming people as a whole. Some means will simply have to be found to bring that farm income up so that farmers generally have their fair share. If they make up 16 per cent of the population, then they are entitled to something like 16 per cent of the national income in Canada. That is the position that we take.
What has that matter to do with the question in point? The serious decline in farm income during the past few years has occurred largely as the result of the problems associated with the production and the marketing of wheat. Everybody knows that with the three bumper crops in a row there were created problems which made it exceedingly difficult to keep farm cash income at a level that would make it possible for the farmers to enjoy prosperity and to buy the goods that are flowing from the factories. The failure of this government to establish markets and to take advantage of market situations that were available throughout the world has materially complicated the farm income situation.
I remember when the Minister of Trade and Commerce scorned the idea of accepting soft currency to a limited extent in return for wheat. I remember when he said, "No; no (country would be prepared to deal on a basis

of that kind". Many foolish things were said at that time also about Britain being unprepared to buy our wheat and to pay for it to a certain degree in pounds sterling.
The fact now is that Japan, Israel, Sweden and a number of other countries have already accepted substantial amounts of wheat from the United States and have been able to pay for it in their own currencies, which currencies were left in their countries to be invested to help them to bring up production of those things which the people in the United States would want to buy.
It has been admitted in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that our wheat marketing situation in Canada has been complicated to a large degree by the methods that are being used by the United States. That is one of them. There is no reason in the world why Canada should not have been preserving her position as the outstanding wheat country in the world by accepting to a degree those soft currencies. There is also no reason why we should not have been leaving those currencies on deposit in those countries from which we are prepared to accept it in order to help those countries to bring up production of the things which Canada would want to buy, and there are plenty of them. But we sit still and say no, we are only going to accept one thing, cash or hard currency, United States dollars under the Bretton Woods agreement. As a consequence we find ourselves taking a back seat to some of these other countries because we are not courageous in our trade outlook. We seem to be frightened to death about trying something new, something other countries are perfectly willing to try and make succeed. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that has complicated our situation in this country to a very great degree, and has accounted to some extent for the decline in our farm income.
One could easily say, of course, that we are raising too much wheat. I suppose under present policies of marketing maybe, but if we are, and if the government at the same time is not going to use any vision and imagination in its marketing policies and in devising new means to get our wheat into the hands of people who need it and want to use it, then it seems to me the next best thing would be for us to encourage our people in the diversification of farming operations. One means of encouraging them to diversify their farming operations would be to have them use irrigation water, and that is exactly the kind of thing envisioned in the protest now before the house.
Saskatchewan has had a very difficult time for many years. Without question Saskatchewan is the greatest wheat province in

Canada, but there are years when Saskatchewan has a most difficult time when the lands become parched because of drought. When the lands of the wheat area are parched the farmers suffer and production is practically nil.
One way to help that situation is to make use of our water resources, and the building of the South Saskatchewan dam would make it possible to water thousands of fertile acres in that province that are capable of producing some of the finest foodstuffs in the world. I draw your attention to the fact, Mr. Speaker, that years ago the Lethbridge area in southern Alberta was about the same as the southern Saskatchewan area. It was subject to these frequent drought cycles, and when they came that part of the country was very hard hit and the people felt it. But years ago we took advantage of the possibilities that were available to us to develop our water resources in that province. We developed large irrigation areas surrounding the city of Lethbridge; and for the past several years now, as a consequence of what has been done in the development of irrigation, the per capita income tax payment of the people of the city of Lethbridge to the government has topped that of every other city in Canada. Why? Simply because Lethbridge is in the very centre of a large irrigated area, and the irrigation farming that goes on in that area contributes dollars year in and year out.
There is very little, if any, failure, because of the stabilizing influence of the water on the soil. If one cares to look into the record he can find recent reports in such magazines as Western Business indicating how important that area has become in the production of foods, especially garden crops. It is expected that within the next few years a $70 million a year frozen vegetable industry will be centred in the city of Lethbridge and its immediate vicinity. There are now several fairly large plants that are processing garden vegetables like peas, beans, carrots, broccoli and that sort of thing. Experts say that the long hours of sunshine, the quality of the soil and the abundance of water in that area make it possible to produce the finest peas in the world.
The same thing could be said of southern Saskatchewan. The soil is not different. It has the long hours of sunshine, and I often wish we could get some of it while we are here in Ottawa. Perhaps the deficit after this year will be about $80 million, and someone might say, "Why should we spend so much money to help the farmers on the prairies in western Canada, in the event of crop failure, when we do not spend sums of money like that for farmers in other parts of Canada?"
Or the fishermen.

The answer is that, bearing in mind what is being done for other parts of Canada, this has been considered fair for the prairie section of western Canada. We are building a great nation, and this can be done only by all parts being willing to support those things they believe are good for the country as a whole. This cannot be

done by listening to sectional appeals, and to those who say, "We are against this, because it does not put anything in the pockets of our people; however, we are prepared to do this other thing because it does put money in the pockets of our people." Do that, if you wish, but do not go out and misrepresent your vote in the country.
People in glass houses.

The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) has referred to people in glass houses. I absolutely defy him to show any time in my political life that I have misrepresented a vote either in the House of Commons or in the legislature.
What about family allowances?

If we cannot sit in the House of Commons as members who have been elected as honourable and honest men, then I for one would rather stay at home.
I make no apology for voting against this amendment. I do not blame the hon. member for Prince Albert for having moved it, because that is his job as a member of the opposition. It is one of his duties to focus attention on such matters. But, having had some part in the formation of Liberal policy, having played some part at national conventions and council meetings to have things written into the program of that party, I am convinced that I have a duty to perform if I believe that certain things we have decided on should be done. If I can convince my fellow Liberal members that something further should be done, well and good. It can be done most quickly in that way, for then I believe that as a party we will proceed to do it, instead of acting as splinter groups. I realize one could be elected more easily in his own constituency by taking some other course.
However, I believe one has to work in co-operation with others to make any headway in this world. Surely in Canada we must be prepared to work with our fellow citizens from other parts of Canada.
An attack was made upon the Prime Minister. I would like to say just a word about that.
A pretty touchy subject.

It is not touchy at all, I may tell the hon. member for Regina City, for the Prime Minister is a man who has been endorsed by the people of Canada by overwhelming majorities both in 1949 and 1953, and he needs no apology from me.

But he is getting it.
South Saskatchewan River Project

No, he is getting no apology. I am just dealing with the silly attack made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) against that great man, the Prime Minister. I believe the Prime Minister received that great endorsation because the people of Canada know he is a great and broad-minded Canadian who will treat all parts of Canada fairly, whether they be the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario, the prairies or British Columbia. That is why he was so endorsed.
The Prime Minister's attitude in regard to this question concerning which the amendment is moved was that he is not yet convinced that the time has come to recommend immediately going ahead with the project.
I am satisfied that if we in the Liberal party intend to regard ourselves as a great national party we should be ready to support things which concern other parts of the country, and which perhaps are of no particular concern to us personally. Then if we have a good case we can go to the Prime Minister and his advisers with it. If we are to be a national party with a national policy we must be fair to all, and on this basis the time will come when a proposition such as this will be accepted.
I think the results would be much better and quicker; I think there is more hope in a policy like that than to take the attitude that we believe in the Liberal party, that we believe in the Liberal program, but should something come up which does not go at once every inch as far as we would like it to go, then we will vote against it. For example, there was the recent great disaster in western Canada, in Saskatchewan in particular, from flooding. Our provincial representatives are here today asking for help because they consider they are part of Canada. In all these matters there should be a national approach, not a narrow provincial approach.
It is on that basis that we can hope to appeal to our fellow Canadians to give us a fair deal in all things. One of the reasons I am happy at all times to support the Prime Minister is that I have implicit faith in his sincere desire as a fair-minded and great Canadian to be fair to all parts of Canada.
I am ready to show that I have faith in him, and I am not ready to withdraw that faith in connection with any individual item as long as he gives the leadership he has given to our country in the last seven years, when it has gone ahead by leaps and bounds. We have prospered and other parts of the country have prospered. A policy has been

The defeat of the government at this time would endanger the budget, with its reduction in taxes. It would endanger the governmental attitude toward tariffs. There is pressure for tariff protection from different parts of the country to help the unemployment situation in those areas, but that pressure has been resisted for the good of all Canada. What kind of a westerner would I be if I turned against a government which has taken a stand on things like that?
Then there are the fiscal agreements. I wonder what Saskatchewan would do without those fiscal agreements, if they were not maintained in force. There are people in Canada today who take a narrow regional attitude, and who would be ready to do away with these fiscal agreements under which we as a province get, without collecting a bit of taxation ourselves, a total of $26 million. To raise that amount of money we would have to put oppressive taxation on our people. Am I to vote on a regional basis and endanger such things as these? Tomorrow someone might ask why they should pay taxes for the people in Saskatchewan, and where would we in Saskatchewan be without these agreements? I have no compunction in saying that under our system of government I support the government. I am proud to support the government which has stood against pressures to increase tariffs and do away with these fiscal agreements.
The hon. member who made this attack on the Prime Minister has indicated that the Prime Minister placed obstacles in the way of progress. What did he mention? He mentioned health insurance and unemployment. As to unemployment, the Liberal party has put forward in its budget and its expanding trade policy measures which have brought about less unemployment than there would be under any other system. Then the Prime Minister has taken the attitude-
How about getting back to the dam?
I am dealing with the question involved in this amendment which is a lack of confidence in the government.
No, it is the dam; we want to hear about the dam.

Apparently the hon. member has not been listening to my remarks. I am showing why I do not propose to support this amendment, and for the moment I am dealing with unemployment. I was about to go on to say that the proposition put forward


by the Prime Minister was a definite step forward in dealing with this problem. He said that you cannot separate the unemployables from the employables and begin to batter these people back and forth. He made the suggestion that they should all be dealt with in a proper way, with Canadians sharing the burden on a fair basis as among the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities. In my opinion that is a definite and humanitarian step forward.
That is what the Prime Minister suggested, and then the hon. member for Assiniboia actually had the colossal nerve to say that a forward and humanitarian step like this indicates that the Prime Minister is not in favour of progress.
Then there is the question of health insurance. What is the attitude there? It is that the provinces must agree in this matter because it is under provincial jurisdiction. My hon. friends opposite get very impatient with that argument but the fact that they are impatient with that argument is the reason they will never get into power in Canada.
Oh, oh.

I have more proof of the decline of the C.C.F. than my hon. friends have. If you take the attitude that the provinces are to be overridden, that their voices are not to be listened to in any way in connection with matters within their jurisdiction, then that is bound to happen. Most people in this country believe in our federal system of government. They believe in the basis upon which we were established as a nation, so much so that they will not support a party that is ready to ignore the provinces in that way. The only way we will make progress is by persuading people in all parts of Canada that progress is necessary and desirable.
I well remember the attitude of our former leader in regard to old age pensions. He took the attitude-

hesitate to interrupt any hon. member. In my opinion the hon. member who has the floor is perfectly within his rights in listing what he regards as the possible consequences of the passage of this amendment, and using those as reasons for voting against the amendment. Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling. There are just two other points I wish to make. I said something about being satisfied and proud to support the Liberal party. I took some part in the convention of 1948. I was on the resolutions committee, and we spent four days working out the resolutions. If anyone will examine what this government has done in carrying out the resolutions passed at that convention, they will find that the government has carried out substantially every one of them.
So far as I am concerned, this is the only party that does make this national appeal. I had some part in getting some of those resolutions adopted. I feel that if anyone who belongs to the Liberal party can get a resolution adopted by the Liberal party they are really accomplishing something worth while, because the Liberal party is a national party and they are getting those things adopted as part of the program of the governing party. So I have no hesitation in saying on this particular matter that I feel it my duty, as a person who believes that the Liberal policy has been good for Canada as a whole, certainly good as a whole for western Canada, to vote to maintain the government in office. In regard to the dam, I would say this.
You are back to that.
I am dealing with the amendment of my hon. friend.
Good.

I was going to say with regard to the question of the dam that I am very much in favour of it, and I hope that in the not too distant future the government will decide to go ahead with the dam. But I do point out to my hon. friend opposite, in the first place, that if the C.C.F. government had not got a report from Professor Cass-Beggs which threw doubt upon the feasibility of the dam on the ground that electricity could be generated more cheaply from the use of natural gas and perhaps later from atomic energy; if they had not sent forward that report to the federal government and left it with them without any suggestion that they disagreed with it, I doubt very much that a royal commission would ever have been appointed, and I think the dam would have been under construction at the present time. The C.C.F. government employed Cass-Beggs and then sent forward that report without
South Saskatchewan River Project any comments whatever, certainly not indicating that they disagreed with it until months later.
It ill behooves the members of that party, the ones who really threw the monkey wrench into this proposition, to make as much fuss about it as they have. I was asked on the floor of the legislature whether I objected to Cass-Beggs expressing these honest opinions of his about the dam, if it were true that this was worth only as much from the standpoint of development as he thought it was; whether it was the right thing that they should send it forward. I admit that it was the right thing to send it forward. But they are the authors of that step. That is one of the things that must be borne in mind by every member from Saskatchewan.
The provincial government is proposing to spend over $70 million on the project. Personally I hope the day will come when a dam will be built without any such colossal expenditure like that by the provincial government. If the provincial government were to use that money in draining northern areas, building roads into that great mineral-bearing part of the province, and otherwise opening up that area, $70 million would enable a considerable amount of work to be done in generally opening up our province. When the time comes to go ahead with this project I hope some sort of arrangement can be worked out whereby the province of Saskatchewan, with its limited financial resources, will not have to pay $70 million odd into it, that it will be a national project in much larger measure than is suggested today by the premier of Saskatchewan.
I am looking at this question as a member from Saskatchewan; thinking what a load of debt such an expenditure could put on the people of our province-less than a million people-and what must be done in regard to building roads and opening up our great north country. We have the same type of north country as have northern Quebec and northern Ontario. We cannot afford to overspend a single dollar. My hope is that when the time comes to build this proposed dam it will be done as a national proposition, without the province of Saskatchewan being asked to invest any more than half of the amount proposed at the present time.
So, Mr. Speaker, without any hesitation I say I am very pleased to show that I have confidence in the government by voting against this motion, the carrying of which would defeat the government and necessitate its resignation or a general election, which I do not think my constituents want, which I do not think Saskatchewan wants, and which I am sure Canada as a whole does not want.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment very briefly on this motion. I intend to support the motion of the hon. member for Prince Albert. I intend to do so, first, because I think the dam would be beneficial to my constituency; second, because I think it would be good for my province; and third, because I think it would be good for the whole dominion of Canada.
I listened with a good deal of interest this afternoon to the arguments of the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Rosthern. I must admit that the hon. member for Rosthern had considerable courage in saying what he did this afternoon, because in Saskatchewan it does take courage to vote against a motion of this kind. Nevertheless, I simply could not follow his reasoning. If this dam is good for the people of Saskatchewan and of Canada-and I think the member would agree that it is-I do not see how he can speak in favour of it on the one hand, and then the next moment vote against it.
Perhaps an argument can be made that the party system requires such a vote. But, as the hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out, even if our Saskatchewan Liberal members did vote for this project, the government would still have a majority of more than 100. So I cannot see that there would be any danger of the government being upset simply because those members supported the amendment. In Saskatchewan today this issue is not a political one. Everyone, whether he is a Liberal, a Conservative, a C.C.F.'er or a Social Crediter, favours the South Saskatchewan dam. I know the Minister of Agriculture favours it. I know that for years he has tried to sell the project to the government. I wish he had been a little more successful.
In the western United States today there is a very serious drought. In Colorado, Wyoming, Oklahoma and other states the dust is blowing daily. Every year for the last three years the drought area has crept further north. It is quite true that on the prairies today it is fairly wet, but we know that dry years may return.
Many members of this house are inclined to feel that the Saskatchewan river dam is just another handout for our province. I should like to impress on them that in my opinion it is not. The Prime Minister is doubtful as to whether or not it is economically feasible. I am absolutely convinced that this dam is economically feasible. It is a self-liquidating project that would pay for itself over a number of years.
Time and time again.

During the depression we paid out millions of dollars in relief funds. Much of this expenditure could be avoided, if another depression came, by having this dam in the middle of the dust area. It would provide a basis for new industries, canneries and the like. It would provide hydroelectric power. The dam would enable many more people to live in Saskatchewan. It would provide new crops and give stability to the livestock industry. I repeat that this irrigation project is not a handout to Saskatchewan. It is a scheme which is sensible, feasible and desirable.
I am sometimes surprised when I realize that countries like Israel, Egypt, India and some of the so-called backward nations in this world can do so much in the way of irrigation, yet a modern prosperous country like Canada lets huge quantities of water run right through the dust bowl into Hudson bay. Over a period of years I suppose this project might cost the people of Canada about $10 million annually, or even about $12 million a year. But the return would be fabulous as compared with the original investment.
To you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house I suggest that this dam could be the making of Saskatchewan. I hope that all members, regardless of their party, will give it the consideration it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we have heard a number of speeches which I thought were quite interesting, to say the least. The Minister of Agriculture spent some time in lecturing hon. members about playing politics with the South Saskatchewan river dam. I wondered just who started this political football. After all, the manner in which this subject has been treated by the government would indicate that that is what they consider it to be. It was started by the Minister of Agriculture himself. He has stated on more than one occasion that he was the first even to mention the project. Certainly from a political standpoint the Minister of Agriculture has used the South Saskatchewan river dam in every election since 1945. He mentioned the year 1946, but I can recall references to the dam being made in the 1945 election campaign.
And in 1944.
The hon. member for Saskatoon informs me that they were talking about the dam in 1944.
Provincially.

Suffice it to say that this matter has been brought to the attention of this country for a great number of years. With

respect to the original proposition, may I say that it was to be a federal undertaking. I was quite interested this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Rosthern make the rounds and complete the circle. He is now back to the position where he says the project should be a federal matter.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I said that under the present proposal we were going to spend over $70 million in the province of Saskatchewan. I said it seemed to me that we should not be expected to spend, as the provincial share, more than half that amount.

Taking the statement just made by the hon. member for Rosthern, Mr. Speaker, might I remind him that it was the federal government that first insisted on the province of Saskatchewan paying anything. Here is the amazing situation. The people of Saskatchewan had been led to believe that the federal government was going to undertake the construction of a dam on the South Saskatchewan river. No one in Saskatchewan had any idea whatsoever that the provincial government was going to be asked to play a part in the construction of the dam.
A few years later, after the federal officials had been pressed by various organizations in the province of Saskatchewan to do something about the dam, they turned around and said, "We are all set to go ahead on the dam, but we are waiting on the provincial government of Saskatchewan to tell us how much they are going to pay as their share of the cost".
If the hon. member for Rosthern is worried about the amount of money the people of Saskatchewan are going to have to pay in connection with the construction of this dam, I suggest that it was his own party and the Minister of Agriculture who first threw on the shoulders of the provincial government any financial responsibility whatever. The year 1949 was the first time the province of Saskatchewan were informed by the federal authorities that they were going to be called upon to pay a share of the cost of the dam.
The hon. member for Rosthern also made a number of other extremely interesting statements. At the outset he said he was not going to apologize for the way he was going to vote. He then proceeded to spend the rest of his time doing just that. However, we heard a speech which many of us have heard a good many times in the past. It was a speech on the grand old Liberal party and the great contribution it is making toward Canadian unity. Of course we in Saskatchewan have heard that type of address so many times that one can perhaps attribute some of the lack of success of Liberal candidates in
South Saskatchewan River Project that province to the playing of this record over and over again ad nauseam.
I noticed that the hon. member, until his closing remarks, made no statement in support of the dam. I should have thought he, as a member from Saskatchewan, would have availed himself of the time at his disposal in this debate to try to persuade hon. members of the importance of an immediate start on the construction of this dam.
Instead of doing that he indulged in something which I think is quite common among Liberals from our province. They rise in their places and rather intimidate members of the opposition. They make this suggestion: "You people should not say much about your own province because, after all, you have certain concessions"-as they would put it-"that you are in danger of losing unless you go along the line and accept our offer, whatever it might be". Mention was made of the P.F.A.A. and the suggestion was "You people from Saskatchewan should not say very much about this dam because you are getting some special privilege".
I want to remind the hon. member for Rosthern of the fact that we are Canadians, whether we come from Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, British Columbia or any other province; and it is a little bit annoying at times to hear Saskatchewan Liberals get to their feet and suggest that we in Saskatchewan are a separate group and that we are existing by leave of the other provinces of Canada.
I suggest that we must consider the South Saskatchewan irrigation project as a national project. Because it happens to be located in the province of Saskatchewan is one reason we from Saskatchewan are more familiar with it than are others. In all sincerity I suggest to the members of this house that naturally members coming from a particular province are better acquainted than are others with particular projects in their own province. Hence it is only natural that when these matters are raised in the House of Commons it is going to be local people who draw them to the attention of other members of the house. Just because we do that is not to suggest that we consider the South Saskatchewan river dam project as something that is going to affect the province of Saskatchewan only.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we must think as Canadians. We must get over the provincialism displayed here this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosthern. He did not call it provincialism; oh, no. He portrayed himself as the great champion of national unity. But by implication and in the very remarks he made he revealed himself as a provincially-minded member because, in

South Saskatchewan River Project effect, what he said was this: "This project affects the people of Saskatchewan only; therefore if you do not mind your p's and q's we are not going to get it; the rest of Canada is not going to give it to us".
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia, we have supported worthwhile projects in all parts of Canada. We have given our full support to the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. No member of this group has failed to give complete support to the building of the Canso causeway. All these projects are in the national interest, and as Canadians we support them. By the same token I suggest that the South Saskatchewan river dam project, although it is being built in the province of Saskatchewan, is of national importance. After all, the economic well-being of one province-and it does not matter which province it is-affects the economic life of the entire country.
The hon. member for Peace River mentioned some of the advantages that accrued to the southern part of Alberta as the result of irrigation projects. We in Saskatchewan are only too well aware of the fact that we are essentially a one-crop economy. That does not make for economic stability. Certainly the objective all of us should seek is to put the agricultural economy of the province on a sounder basis, and through diversification of agriculture make not only the economic lot of those farming in that area better but add to the economic well-being of people in all parts of Canada.
A number of other comments were made this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosthern, and I should like to make passing reference to one or two of them. He mentioned something about the Prime Minister, and said we in the house should not have the temerity to challenge his wisdom or logic. I suggest that no member is beyond criticism. Because a member happens to belong to the cabinet or be the prime minister I do not think he should therefore be absolved of all blame or free from all criticism.
I suggest that in recent years the Prime Minister has indicated on a number of occasions that he is a thoroughgoing conservative, with a small "c". I believe history will bear that out. Certainly in his attitude of late on a great number of questions he has revealed himself so conservative as to be termed reactionary. I am not going to go into that matter this afternoon, but I do suggest that the Prime Minister as leader of the government must accept the greater responsibility for government action or inaction, and in this case it is inaction.
The Liberals of Saskatchewan talk about their support for the dam, but they support

a party, they support a government, they support a prime minister, all of whom have said "No" to the dam. Now they say they have to hew to the line and vote against the amendment because it involves want of confidence. Another hon. member has already mentioned that with the top-heavy majority enjoyed by the government, defections on the part of hon. members opposite certainly are not going to jeopardize the government. What is more, I suggest the Prime Minister has stated repeatedly that he is anxious to be convinced that this project is in the national interest.
How is he going to come to that conclusion? I suggest hon. members should be in a position where they could reveal to him what they think. Consequently I suggest to hon. members on the government side that this is their opportunity to say to the Prime Minister of Canada that they believe the dam should be built, and no amount of alibiing in advance on the part of Saskatchewan Liberals is going to cover up the fact that in this instance they are placing their party ahead of the South Saskatchewan river dam project.
I mentioned a few moments ago the strange twist of events that has taken place recently. In the initial instance the dam was to be a federal undertaking. Then, in order to get off the hook, the Minister of Agriculture suddenly confronted the province of Saskatchewan with the ultimatum that if they wished to see the dam built they would have to pay part of the cost. Now we have the spectacle of a supporter of the government suggesting that the province has agreed to pay too much. You cannot satisfy these people. In the first instance they complained because the province was not going to pay anything toward the project, and now they turn around and argue that the province has agreed to pay too much. I suggest if the province is offering to pay too much it is up to the hon. member for Rosthern and his colleagues to have a heart to heart talk with the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister and convince them of that fact, if the building of the dam is in the realm of immediate possibility.
We have heard vague assurances that the dam is going to be built some time; that it is going to be built tomorrow. The old, trite saying that tomorrow never comes is applicable in this case. I suggest the government has had ample time to reveal whether or not it ever intends to proceed with the construction of the dam. Being removed from the provincial scene, one misses some of the politicking that is going on in the province. But I can recall that a few years ago the hon. member for Rosthern was leader of the

opposition in the legislature, and he made a great to-do about the Cass-Beggs report. He said they were all set to build the dam, and the Saskatchewan government had a report on power made by David Cass-Beggs which frightened the government into appointing a royal commission.
The royal commission was appointed in 1952, and it held hearings and made a report. Just to make absolutely certain that the commission's report would be what the government wanted, the government appointed as members of the commission Dr. T. H. Hogg of Toronto, a power man, Mr. G. A. Gaherty of Calgary, a power man, and the late Dr. John Widtsoe of Salt Lake City, the only irrigation expert on the royal commission, and the government got precisely what it asked for. It got a report confirming the fears expressed by the Prime Minister that perhaps the project was not in the national interest. Nevertheless the report, in the light of present-day conditions, is quite interesting. At page 29 there is a discussion of the immediate effects upon the economy, and I find there the following:
With relatively full employment, no new physical assets can be created without diverting labour and other resources from their current employment. Society must then do without the production that is lost by this transfer and this represents the real cost to it of the project. When labour and other resources have no employment opportunities they can be utilized for the production of goods and services which thereby are secured without any real cost to the community. This is one aspect of the argument that the best time for heavy investment of public money is during a period of business recession.
Of course I am quite well aware that the government does not consider we are having a business recession. In spite of the efforts of members on the opposition side to convince them that over 600,000 unemployed in Canada represent a serious condition, they have tended to minimize at every turn the economic situation facing the people of the country at the present time. But I do want to refer to a suggestion put forward by one of the government supporters a few moments ago. He said we should not be too impatient, that we should be prepared to wait for this beneficent Liberal government, which has the interests of all Canada at heart-I should put that in quotation marks-to build the dam, and that if we wait long enough some day it will do so.
The suggestion is made that we should not complain because, after all, if federal funds were to be used in building the dam this would be a special concession or favour bestowed on us by a beneficent federal government. I want to suggest at the outset that the greater part of the money to be
South Saskatchewan River Project spent in the building of the dam will not be spent in the province of Saskatchewan at all. In the building of a dam of this magnitude a great portion of the cost will be represented by the buying of heavy machinery, and that machinery is going to be purchased in eastern Canada. It is going to be purchased in places other than the province of Saskatchewan.
As a matter of fact, estimates of as high as 75 per cent have been made of the leakage in projects of this kind. Only a quarter or perhaps less than a quarter of the money actually to be spent on the dam will be spent in the province of Saskatchewan. The bulk of the money will be spent in other parts of Canada, particularly in eastern Canada.
This brings out my point that the project is in the national interest. It will be built, if it ever is built under existing conditions of sharing the cost, largely by the provincial government. The hon. member for Rosthern has suggested that the provincial government has committed itself to spending $70 million toward the completion of the project. It is actually $78 million. According to the latest information the federal government would be called upon to spend about $62 million. This $62 million would be spread over a great number of years to create economic stability in a province that has long known crop failures and drought.
In spite of the fact that there is a great deal of water on the plains today, let us remember that the building of a dam is also a measure of flood control. Let us remember that within the past 10 years there have been times when feed has been imported into the province from Manitoba. We are faced with the problem of building up a measure of economic stability in a part of Canada which, after all, has a great effect on the entire dominion.
Perhaps I should say a word about the role of the Minister of Agriculture in this whole affair. The minister has told us he is in favour of the dam. He has been telling us that for a great number of years, and he still persists in telling us it is going to be built. I have no doubt the dam will be built, but I have serious doubts whether the Minister of Agriculture or any of his colleagues will be on the government benches when that is done. Certainly if we have waited this long to get any evidence of willingness to proceed with this project, then I think we are going to look in vain for any leadership from the Liberal party in this connection.
I do want to suggest that one or two conditions obtain in so far as the Minister of Agriculture is concerned. In the first instance.

South Saskatchewan River Project it the minister did decide to really build the dam, or to look upon the promise to build the dam as more than just an election promise, then he has been guilty of deceiving the people of Saskatchewan over the past 10 or 11 years. If he really believed this dam would be proceeded with by this government, or had any reason to believe the government would listen to his suggestions, then I suggest his influence with the government is almost negligible. I suggest that, as a matter of protest if nothing else, he should have taken issue with his colleagues, realizing his status as a member of the cabinet.
We find a different situation obtains with respect to the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison). They are not ministers of this government, and certainly when this vote is taken there is nothing whatever to stop them from voting for this amendment. They say they would be voting non-confidence in the government. Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out that on a previous occasion in this house the hon. member for Rosthern voted for an amendment of this kind. The adoption of that amendment did not involve the defeat of the government. If these members feel that way, then I suggest the Prime Minister should say to the supporters of the government that on this issue there shall be a free vote; that he wants an expression of opinion on whether or not this project should be proceeded with. I believe that should be done; then the Liberals from Saskatchewan would have no valid ground for saying they must go along with the government on this particular issue.
Balderdash.

The hon. member for Swift
Current-Maple Creek is muttering in his beard again. I would prefer that he be intelligent, but he insists upon being asinine.
I do not want to follow your example.

It is true that I and others have injected an element of politics into the discussion this afternoon. I suggest, however, this project has been made a political football by none other than the members who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker. From the outset the South Saskatchewan dam was promised to the people of Saskatchewan by the Liberal party. Now they find themselves in a position where many people are asking for some results. Just saying over and over again that you are in favour of doing something is a poor substitute for action.

I do want to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the role of the Minister of Agriculture could be briefly summed up in this way. In the negotiations that have been carried on among the federal officials, the P.F.R.A. and the officials of the provincial government to bring about some measure of agreement which would facilitate the commencement of this project, the provincial negotiations have always been at a distinct disadvantage. While they, were negotiating in good faith they never knew whether, as a result of all their negotiation, the federal government would pay any attention to them. It seems to me that if you are going to have negotiations you must have equity; you must have fairness, and you must have two parties willing to sit down and say if we can arrive at some mutually acceptable agreement we are honour bound to proceed under that agreement.
The situation has been that while Mr. Douglas and the members of his cabinet have been carrying on negotiations with the federal government, they were always aware of the fact that even if they were able to come to an agreement on every particular with the federal officials it still did not mean that the dam was going to be built. The provincial government stated in advance that they wanted this dam built. They wanted to meet with federal officials to bring about a solution satisfactory to both sides, and then they wanted an immediate start on the dam. The federal officials would come along and say, "Well, we will talk it over, but that does not mean we are going to build it if we do come to an agreement." Every time an agreement was reached the Minister of Agriculture would pop up with some new condition.
I am not going over the whole story, but at the outset there was some reference to the subsidization of power. Earlier there was a reference to the Cass-Beggs report, and there was a report which had to do with the power aspect of the project. No one can argue any longer that the question of power is an obstacle, under any circumstances, to an agreement between the federal and provincial government. I believe that matter has been taken care of. The statement was made, "We are not going to permit the subsidization of power in any province by the use of federal funds." In order to avoid that the provincial government agreed to pay the full cost of building a power station at the dam.
After that agreement had been reached we had every reason to believe that we were making some progress, but up popped the Minister of Agriculture with another condition. He said the province would have to

pay the cost of moving that water from the reservoir to the users of the water. The province agreed to that. They were going to bend over backward to do everything they possibly could to bring about an agreement which would be acceptable to the federal officials.
Then we were told we had to pay part of the cost of building the reservoir itself. When the hon. member for Rosthern complains that the province is paying too much, I ask him this. Who forced the province into the position of paying too much? I say it was his colleagues, the Minister of Agriculture, the Prime Minister and the Liberal government who forced the province into that position.
There is no use turning around and trying to blame the province, or suggesting they are being unwise and too extravagant in spending that much money, when the fact is that by progressive steps the Liberal government have forced the provincial government in Saskatchewan to commit itself to greater expenditures.
Well, we agreed to pay for part of the reservoir. We thought then we were going to make headway. Along came the Minister of Agriculture, reaching into his pocket and pulling out another document. "Now", he says, "what about the treasury bills?" There had been an agreement that the province might be permitted to pay part of its cost of construction in treasury bills, payable over a term of 20 years. The Minister of Agriculture came along and said, "We think we can sell this idea to the cabinet only if the province agrees to pay it all in cash every year". I am certain they felt virtually certain that the province would be unable to meet that exacting requirement.
Then-the latest-the Minister of Agriculture comes along and says, "What about penstocks?" Well, you cannot but wonder about it; every time you reach the point where the province may get something from the agreement, you find a new and exacting condition put forward. I suggest in all sincerity that these conditions have been put forward as part of deliberate policy on the part of this government, trying to force the government of Saskatchewan into a position where it would refuse to go further. And, if that had happened, the Liberal party would then go up and down the province saying, "Oh, we wanted to build this dam, but the provincial government stood in our way". In my judgment that is precisely the policy pursued by the Minister of Agriculture in the country and in the House of Commons.

And where does he stand in Saskatchewan today?
