The question has been asked as to where he stands in Saskatchewan today. Well, I do not wish to deal with that at length, but there are brandished knives in Saskatchewan among the Liberals who are fighting over a corpse.
I repeat that this whole matter of negotiation between the federal and provincial governments has been on the basis of leading the provincial government along to the point where, it was hoped, that government would go no farther. But, despite all these obstacles and roadblocks thrown in the way of the provincial government, it had been determined to go ahead with the dam. The premier of Saskatchewan repeatedly wrote to Ottawa requesting interviews with the Prime Minister, and saying that something should be done.
Last fall the premier of the province was very anxious to come to Ottawa to meet with the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet. The Prime Minister showed the letter to the Minister of Agriculture, which was the most unfortunate thing that could have happened, because the Minister of Agriculture said, in effect, "Well, I will take care of that. That is all right. I am going out to Saskatchewan next week, and I will take care of it".
So he went out to Saskatchewan, and once again another of these obstacles was thrown before the provincial government which, by this time, was getting a little frustrated and annoyed. They insisted upon coming to terms, and finding out what was the score. Finally the premier of the province had the temerity to inform the Minister of Agriculture that the province of Saskatchewan wanted the Liberal government in Ottawa to say yes or no. Then the Minister of Agriculture turned around and said, "If that is the way you are going to do business, all right. Only last July you insisted upon our committing ourselves when we were not prepared to negotiate. You must know that the only way we can negotiate with you is to have you lay all your cards on the table, and then we will decide whether or not we are playing for keeps."
Well, we know that finally a meeting was held following the preliminary dominion-provincial conference. While I do not know for sure, I believe the Minister of Agriculture was present at that meeting. In any event the sum total of the meeting was a flat no, on the part of the Prime Minister. So, after all these years of promises, and after all this time, here is the situation. Liberal members have been going up and down the province of Saskatchewan making all sorts of promises. Finally, when the chips are down and the premier of Saskatchewan is face to face with

South Saskatchewan River Project the Prime Minister of Canada, the' Prime Minister said what I am certain Liberals must have know many years ago, that this government had no intention whatsoever of building that dam.
I just wish to conclude by reminding hon. members once again that this is not a provincial issue. The building of the South Saskatchewan dam is a national issue, just as is the building of the Canso causeway or the building of the St. Lawrence seaway project. It is something which will have great benefits for the people of Canada as a whole. It is time to build this country up; and when I think that in the province of Saskatchewan, where we have less than a million population, our province has enough faith in the future, enough faith in the building of the dam, that we are willing to put up $78 million, then I certainly think the government of Canada which, at this juncture, would have to put up $62 million, should come through and fulfil its promises, and commence construction of that dam.
I suggest that in voting on this amendment Liberals from Saskatchewan will be able to show their true colours. They will have their opportunity when the vote is taken to let the country know and to let their constituents know whether they are in favour of the dam to the point where they are prepared to put themselves on record to that effect. I challenge Liberal members from Saskatchewan to vote for this amendment.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, shortly before six o'clock the hon. member for Rosthern spent a good deal of time explaining that a vote for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert would mean a vote against the government, and if the motion should carry the government would be defeated. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre interjected and asked the hon. member for Rosthern about his vote on August 27, 1946, when the milk subsidy was before parliament.
I would remind the house that on that occasion the hon. member for Rosthern voted for a similar amendment. The motion was carried but the government was not defeated, and the business of the house went on. I might mention that on that date I had the


pleasure of presenting an amendment on the motion to go into supply, as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be left out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house desires to record its opinion that consideration should be given to the continuance of the milk subsidy so as to ensure adequate return to milk producers and make possible the consumption of milk for the nutrition of the Canadian people without any further increase in the price thereof to the consumers."
The present Prime Minister was the acting prime minister on that occasion and he suggested after our case had been presented that I should withdraw the motion. However, my colleagues and I did not agree, and later the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) asked that hon. members of the house have a free vote. He went on to say, as reported on page 5431 of Hansard:
Therefore I should like to serve notice that if this vote carries the government will immediately move that the house go into committee of supply this day. I believe that that procedure is consistent with the rules, and if there can be general agreement on that point the work of the house can be facilitated and the objective of hon. members attained.
I appreciate the fact that on a number of occasions the Prime Minister has expressed the opinion that public funds for the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam should not be voted by parliament at this particular time. However, I am sure the Prime Minister could not have any objection to testing the opinion of parliament. I am of the opinion at the moment that a majority of the members of the house might agree with the Prime Minister. I think it was a pity this afternoon that the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Rosthern did not take more time to point out the advantages to all Canada of having a project such as this proceeded with.
I shall do that on my estimates.

There is going to be a vote shortly, and I think it would have been desirable that hon. members of all parties have a chance to indicate whether they think the proposal of the hon. member for Prince Albert should be supported. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would be in a much stronger position if he had a favourable vote, as we had when the milk subsidy was before this parliament.
I do not wish to become involved this evening in a political discussion with members across the way, but I do want to present some arguments in an effort to convince the house that this proposal is a desirable step in connection with the development of all Canada. We should not lose sight of the fact

that during the past 25 years we have had two problems which have become national in character, the problem of drought and the present problem of flooding.
I have here the telegraphic crop report for May 11, which is published by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This points out that the average rainfall in Manitoba for the period from April 1 was 2-07 inches as compared with the long-term average of 1 [DOT] 48. That indicates that this is not a serious problem in Manitoba as a whole, although there are a few sections where there has been a sharp increase.

In the case of Saskatchewan the long-term average is 1-21 inches, compared with this year's amount of 3-86 inches. I am sure that hon. members, regardless of where they sit, will not blame any government for the drought experience in the thirties or for the flooding we have had in northeastern Saskatchewan during the past several years. The secretary of a municipality in my constituency writes that the last good crop they had was in 1949, and since that time they have had a succession of floods or frosts or both. He states that as a result, the arrears of taxes which stood at $38,000 in 1949 increased to $51,000 in 1950, to $62,000 in 1951, to $68,000 in 1952, to $80,000 in 1953 and to $116,000 in 1954. This is a municipality with quite a small assessment. It is in an area where they have had a succession of very wet years. This has posed a most difficult problem for the people in that municipality.
I realize that the building of the South Saskatchewan dam is not going to solve the problem for all people in Saskatchewan, but I think the government must decide that a project similar to the Tennessee valley authority should be established in Saskatchewan so
South Saskatchewan River Project we can conserve the excessive moisture we have some years to make it available in the years of drought.
Experts in the various departments of government here do not wish to take responsibility for the sort of weather we have been having. I had a letter from one of my constituents who has been keeping careful weather records for over 50 years, and it is his considered opinion that the atomic and hydrogen bomb tests have been a factor in the most unusual weather we have been having. I might mention that such a well known authority as Dr. Ritchie Calder wrote in the New Statesman, and Nation a few months ago that up until a year ago the best experts laughed at the idea of these experiments having any effect on the weather. But now the best authorities are not so dogmatic. They concede that there might be some connection. My friend writes:
Last year, marked atomic conditions were ameliorated after September 20. The conditions passed to drought (as they had in 1952) as the weeks went by. Winter did not close down at Sub Rosa, 2,000 feet above the sea level, until November 26, a month later than normal, and drought continued all winter and onwards.
. . . the drought continued on into spring (which came at the abnormally early date, for the hills, of April 3.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; this seems a long way from the South Saskatchewan dam.

It is not so very far, Mr. Speaker. My constituent has expressed the opinion-and it is not an isolated opinion- that the atomic and hydrogen bomb tests have had an effect on the weather. If the hon. member for Vancouver South, who is an authority on a great many subjects, will say definitely that they have not, I am sure some of the other well known scientists in the world will be glad to have his considered opinion.

A very serious problem is developing as a result of the excessive rainfall which I have mentioned, as recorded by the Department of Trade and Commerce in this bulletin on weather conditions in the prairie provinces. This publication suggests that there are areas which are having very heavy rainfalls each year. This poses a problem which is too great for the municipalities to deal with, and it is becoming a problem that is too great for the province.
I appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister and his cabinet are negotiating with cabinet ministers from Saskatchewan to

South Saskatchewan River Project review this whole problem, but I believe we could not start too soon appropriating funds for a project such as the South Saskatchewan dam. The cost that has been mentioned probably sounds a good deal as compared with the projects we had a few years ago. But as compared with some of the projects we undertook during the war it seems a very modest amount. The Minister of Trade and Commerce embarked on the construction of the Polymer project at Sarnia when we lost our supplies of natural rubber. This project required an investment of over $50 million, with no guarantee that the completed project would meet our requirement. The Shipshaw project was also undertaken. These did not place any great strain on the Canadian economy.
I submit that the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam, as a beginning to conserve moisture and make water available in areas where they have had recurring droughts, is a step that must be taken. Consider the large expenditures we are able to make in the field of defence. The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) was good enough to take about 40 of his colleagues to the north of his constituency a short time ago, and they were greatly impressed by the achievements in that north country.
These expenditures are made in the public interest. We were all greatly impressed by those large planes that were being used to transport heavy equipment to the north. We were told that the heavy Caterpillars could travel under their own power into the bowels of one of these big machines. They told us that the machines weighed 50 tons empty, and could take off with a load of 50 tons without any trouble. The machine empty represented an investment of a little less than $3 million. I realize that the Canadian government has not made the investment, but we are participating in the use of these very large machines.
When one considers the importance of the dam to our whole economy, and particularly to people in the area that would be served by it, I think it is only reasonable that we should test public opinion in this parliament tonight. I think the Prime Minister will agree tonight, as he did in 1946, that members regardless of where they sit, should stand up and indicate whether or not they think the building of this dam would be serving the best interests of Canada. We should not lose sight of the fact that if we are not prepared to conserve our land and water resources and use them in the best interests of all the people of Canada and all the people of the world, we cannot forever look forward to holding this vast territory.

I would remind the house that the Euphrates valley at one time supported a population of over 20 million people. Now only 2j million people live there, illiterate, ill-clothed, ill-fed, diseased peasants, who eke out a wretched existence. They did not have the advantage of all the information that we have available. As the hon. member for Prince Albert has suggested, I believe we should immediately start on the construction of this one project in an area in Canada which has produced great quantities of food for the country, an area that is vital to the continued prosperity of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I think the discussion of this particular subject is very timely when we consider the state of affairs in western Canada. People are certainly frustrated by the apathy of this government in not going ahead with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam. I do not believe I could think of one other proposal that has been used to greater advantage as a political football by the Liberals, with the possible exception of the Hudson Bay railway, than this proposal of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
At present the situation in western Canada is the result of a combination of factors. I do not believe we are going to find a solution to this problem unless we are prepared to undertake some kind of flood control. I do not believe the topography of the land in Saskatchewan is able to handle such severe conditions of flooding as we have had during the past few years. I do not believe the river channels and watercourses are able to cope with that flooding. I believe we have to undertake as a dominion project some sort of over-all water conservation policy in this region.
I should like to go even further. I suggest that possibly we should give some consideration to a scheme of diverting acreage. If a farmer had a few acres of land on his farm that was eroding very badly the government should make some concession for that land if he took it out of production and planted it to grass, for instance, or if he did a little drainage work, and took those acres out of production. I think it would go a long way toward the over-all water conservation program we must have in this country if we are going to solve the problem with which we will be confronted in the future.
So I say the problem with which we are faced is a climax to a condition which has come about over the past few years. Certainly the leader of the Social Credit party this afternoon expressed what a great many of us feel, I suppose, that we have so much water we do not know what to do with it,

and we do not like to hear the word mentioned. That is true. But when we examine this proposition of water control, I think that in itself will help to remedy this flooding condition with which we are confronted. I believe the dam would be one of the keys to this over-all water conservation program of which I spoke.
I will not say I was annoyed, but I was a little bit concerned this afternoon when the Minister of Agriculture stated that the dam had not been known as such prior to 1946, or words to that effect. Since I have been in this house I have been amazed, on every occasion this subject has been discussed, to hear members of the government and other hon. members opposite go out of their way to try to convince not only other members of the Liberal party but Canadians in general that we in Saskatchewan, because we are clamouring for this dam, have some selfish motive, or some motive that is not in the interests of the rest of Canada.
I am sure we must all agree that if we could build the dam it would not only be of the greatest assistance in controlling water in Saskatchewan, but would help immeasurably in controlling the flow of water in the province of Manitoba. When we take these factors into consideration, to say nothing of the proposal that was put forward this afternoon by the hon. member for Regina City and by other members on this side of the house at various times, as to the public investment program that such a proposition would initiate, I think it is something that should be given the greatest consideration when we are speaking about building the dam as being in the national interest.
I should like to place on record one or two statements that have been made. As I said a moment ago, it is not only the Minister of Agriculture who has used this issue. He said this afternoon that he wanted to see the dam built. May I say that I am in complete agreement with that statement. It seems to me that not only the minister but every other Liberal from the province of Saskatchewan has used this issue whenever he felt it was politically advantageous to do so. I should like to place on record one or two quotations which I believe justify that assertion.
First of all, even back in 1945 the Minister of Agriculture, while speaking to a meeting at Southey, had this to say:
Southey, Sask. Agriculture minister Gardiner told an election meeting last night that plans are ready for starting prairie farm rehabilitation projects costing $30 million.
This work for irrigation could be started as soon as the need for employment arose after the war. In addition the minister told of a large program
South Saskatchewan River Project for which the plans were only partly drawn, costing $110 million in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It would involve a dam on the Saskatchewan river near Outlook, Saskatchewan.
That was one of the statements made. I am sure all the provocative statements have been made by Liberals themselves. Those of us in Saskatchewan cannot be accused of going out and making the only provocative statements that have been made in this connection.
Again I should like to quote Mr. Charles Henderson, then Liberal member of parliament, speaking at Kindersley on May 18, 1945. Among other things he stated as follows:
. .	. that he had secured assurances that $111
million would be available for the proposed scheme.
He was speaking of the South Saskatchewan river dam.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Neither one of those statements was with regard to the South Saskatchewan river dam alone. They were with regard to all the large projects. More than half of the projects are already completed.
This quotation of which I am speaking definitely had reference to the South Saskatchewan river dam.
I was speaking about the $110 million proposal which, as was pointed out in the previous quotation, was for all the projects.

That is true, but the dam was to be included in that expenditure. Then Mr. J. Gordon Ross, then member for Moose Jaw, speaking at Chaplin on May 23, 1946, in preparation for the Morse by-election, had this to say, speaking of this expenditure:
. . . and a start will be made as soon as men and. equipment are available.
He was referring to the South Saskatchewan irrigation scheme. Then on October 20, 1948, the Minister of Agriculture, speaking about the dam at Allan, Saskatchewan, and this to say:
Most of the money would be provided by the federal government because it could not be expected that Saskatchewan, subject to drought, could carry the load of such a capital expenditure.
Then we have the statement made by the hon. member for Rosthern in support of Mr. Boucher. He advocated the election of Mr. Boucher if the people of Saskatchewan wanted to get the dam built.
He added, "You certainly won't get anywhere by sending C.C.F'ers to Ottawa-

Hear, hear.

South Saskatchewan River Project
That is all right. But where are these great champions of the dam today?
Right here.

Then there are other statements by the Minister of Agriculture. They go on .and on. I am not going to read from them .any further, but I wanted to put on the record some of the very provocative state-aments that have been made from time to .time, as I say, whenever the Liberals thought .it was politically advantageous to do so.
Besides the value of the dam as a water .conservation measure, and besides its importance as a power and irrigation project, I think one of the things we must bear in mind is that in the Carrot river triangle there js in the neighbourhood of-and I shall be conservative

750,000 acres of land which .could be utilized provided it was drained; and it will never be settled until complete drainage is carried out. That situation can come about only when we have on the South Saskatchewan river the control that would be provided if we had the dam there. I therefore say that power and irrigation are only part of the great advantages that would be gained from that proposition.
I think there are a great many aspects of [DOT]this matter of flooding in Saskatchewan that should be brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture as well as to other members of the house. Over the last few days I have had a great many letters from farmers who have grain stored in bins out in the field. Because of the flooding, great loss is going to take place in connection with that grain. These farmers are not able to haul their grain. They cannot get it out. To start with, there is no room in the elevators. The roads are impassable. That grain is going to be a complete loss in many cases. I think that is a deplorable situation.
As was pointed out this afternoon in connection with the unemployment question, the money spent in building this dam would be of the greatest importance to the over-all economy of this country. The fact that 75 per cent of the money spent on the turbines and all other materials that would be used in the construction would accrue to other parts of Canada should be given some weight when this question is being considered in the light of how it is going to affect the over-all economy of the country.
This afternoon somebody asked, what has this to do with the over-all economy? How would this be beneficial in the national interest? I should like to point out, as I have on previous occasions, that we in western Canada have supported the seaway, though 1 do


not think too many of our farmers are completely taken in by the promises of what is going to accrue to them when the seaway is completed. I think it has been overexaggerated. In my opinion a great many people believe that in all probability freight rates in western Canada will increase when the seaway is completed. They are going to increase for the very simple reason that in all likelihood freight revenues in eastern Canada are going to decline. The railways will have to be subsidized, and the only place that is going to be done is at the expense of the western farmers. Nevertheless I believe there are very few farmers who are not in complete agreement with the seaway project.
Therefore I think we should look at these things in the light of the national interest. This afternoon reference was made to the proposition made years ago. I am not going to elaborate further, because the matter was well covered this afternoon by one or two other speakers. I should merely like to say that first of all the dam was to be built as a wholly federal project. Then Saskatchewan agreed to pay $33 million toward the project. Then we were asked and agreed to pay as high as $45 million. The next figure was $65 million and now it is $78 million, but we are no closer to getting the dam now than we were before. As a matter of fact the people of Saskatchewan feel they have been betrayed and led down the "Gardiner" path.

Since my hon. friend has brought my name into it, as a matter of privilege I wish to say that we have never asked the Saskatchewan government to pay $78 million toward the South Saskatchewan river dam at any time.
That is because you will not agree to build it.

The minister said this afternoon the Liberals would build the dam, so we are back now exactly where we were when the proposition was first talked about. I should like to emphasize that I believe now is the time we should give the greatest consideration to an over-all national policy of water conservation. I think the South Saskatchewan dam is the key to that over-all policy. There are other projects which I am sure would be just as important, but I think it is important that we get away from this narrowness, this provincialism, when we are speaking about the South Saskatchewan river dam. In my opinion it should be part and parcel of an over-all program if we are to have any degree of flood control in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time particularly to point out that the position this party has taken on the numerous occasions we have raised this question has emphasized the fact that this is not something exclusively of concern to the province of Saskatchewan. This is not merely a matter of debate between the Minister of Agriculture on the one hand and those from Saskatchewan in different parties on the other. The remark by the previous speaker with regard to provincialism would certainly not apply, and I am not suggesting he intended it to apply, to the position we have taken with respect to the matter since it has been first discussed. There is just a little tendency to carry on the debate as though this were something Saskatchewan was seeking to obtain from the government through the kind offices of the Minister of Agriculture, who happens to come from that province.
I am not going to repeat in detail the speeches I have made previously on this very subject. It happens to be a subject with which I have had certain personal acquaintance over many years. I can recall that for a great many years it has been one of the projects that has arrested the attention of those who believe that by the combined action of the governments of this country we should develop these great undeveloped resources, particularly where there is a strong humanitarian demand. I doubt if, from the humanitarian point of view, there is a single project now awaiting development in Canada that compares in importance with the development of the South Saskatchewan dam.
I am convinced this is a practical project. Certainly the evidence is there from engineers whose skill, competence and judgment would not be questioned by the Minister of Agriculture, because they are holding their offices as the result of his approval. Engineers of his own department have examined the project, have reported that it is practical, and have stated that it should proceed.
To those who are not acquainted with this matter the question might naturally arise as to why, with that recommendation before them, the government do not see fit to act. It may be well for those who may not have followed the matter to recall the rather strange arguments put forward by the government from time to time with regard to royal commissions. When we have asked that the government do what any big business would do and appoint a royal commission to examine the over-all organization of government and the efficiency of government
3817
South Saskatchewan River Project administration from the ordinary departmental administrative point of view, we have been told that this would be a denial of the responsibility of government. But we have seen just recently that the government proposes to set up a commission on the general economy of Canada. They have already named the chairman of the commission.
In the present case, because it is convenient to them, it is not a denial of responsibility. In the particular case under discussion they had the recommendation of qualified engineers who worked on the spot, carried out their tests right near the Coteau creek site, and after careful examination and research found that the project could be developed economically and in a practical way. But then the government, which is so very anxious about royal commissions which might impinge upon their responsibility, decided that it had a way out, and so it would not have to act on the advice of the engineers under the Minister of Agriculture, who obviously have his approval because they are still employed, the government appointed a royal commission to act as a burial squad. That is what it has been, nothing else.
They did not appoint a royal commission at the time they proceeded with the St. Lawrence seaway development and joined in that great co-ordinated enterprise which involves many times the expenditure that would be involved in the South Saskatchewan dam. They relied on their own engineers, men who were similarly responsible to a department of government, men who also carried out their duties, just as the engineers answerable to the Minister of Agriculture did. Why did they need a royal commission for a much smaller enterprise, though it is an enterprise of immense importance to the people of Saskatchewan? They did so for no other reason than to find an excuse for delay; that was the only reason. They had the engineers' report, just as they had the reports on the St. Lawrence development.
In this case we should not become too much involved in the details as between the power and irrigation. We know there is an estimate of the development of a minimum of 150,000 horsepower. We know part of that power will be required for the pumping machines which will be necessary to carry out the great irrigation project which will make one of the most arable areas in Saskatchewan in the neighbourhood of Outlook. There is no uncertainty as to what the soil is going to be like once the irrigation goes through. Those who have visited the experimental development near Outlook have seen some of the richest soil anywhere in the prairie provinces, through the simple device
3818	HOUSE OF
South Saskatchewan River Project of irrigation carried out for the one purpose of determining what the result would be of going ahead with this development. There is, therefore, no uncertainty.
As a matter of fact there was no uncertainty in the mind of the minister last year, because on June 10 the Minister of Agriculture was reported in the Regina Leader-Post as saying this. I ask hon. members on the other side as well as on this-perhaps on the other side more than on this, because we know we must convince them if there is any chance of a favourable vote on this important motion-to listen to what the minister said last year:
We have been doing all right at clearing obstruction out of the way. There were four when we started discussions and there is now only the one left-the question of power development costs-
Well, that simplifies it. All they need to know is the question of power development costs. They have the engineers. They have the reports. They know what can be done. I am convinced that the people in the rest of Canada want this project carried out and are prepared to provide from the common funds of the Dominion of Canada whatever is appropriately required under agreement with Saskatchewan to carry out this vitally important project.
This is not a provincial matter. This is one of those developments that will have its impact upon the whole of Canada. It is not only the people of Saskatchewan who have reason for great concern that today, in this country which has seen such remarkable developments within the last few years, there is within that part of the Palliser triangle near the area that would be served by the water and the power produced in this way as desolate a scene as we are likely to see anywhere in Canada.
Not long ago in New York I saw a collection of photographs that I would commend to anyone who happens to find his way there. It is a collection from all over the world, and can be seen in the new art gallery in New York. One of the pictures that struck me very forcibly was a picture of three dejected looking children leaning on a fence. There was a scene of dust, dryness and desolation behind them, and up on a hill in the central background was a none too attractive house. As I looked at the picture I was under the impression that it was probably a picture from the dust bowl in the United States. I then saw it was from Canada, from this very area that would be served by this development. Churches have been abandoned; schools have been abandoned; homes have been abandoned in an area with


soil that would produce crops as good as could be found anywhere on the prairies if this project were undertaken.
I am not suggesting that the government make capital expenditures recklessly. Nevertheless the human equation is an important factor in this matter. The simple decision to proceed with this, not just repeated assurances that we are getting further along the road toward removing the obstructions, would have a tremendous effect on people who see little opportunity of return for their early work, if they are still on the farm, and who see little prospect for their children on that land.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the evidence is there that this can be done. The evidence is there that the project would have a profound effect upon that whole area. The 150,000 horsepower is not by any manner of means the figure that should be in the minds of the members of this house in asking for a decision on this subject, a subject which has been bandied back and forth for years, which has been one of continuing promise by the minister and of continuing evasion by the government.
If we believe in the system of government responsibility, then it is time the minister did not suggest he could go out and make one statement independently of the government without being in the position that he should resign if the government fails to back him up on any undertaking on which his promise had been based. It is one or the other. Either he has been making statements recklessly, without due regard to his responsibility to the government, or he had some reason to believe the government would back him up. It is one or the other. It is time he took appropriate action to indicate whether he talked without responsibility or whether the government failed in their responsibility to him. This would clear the air and let us know exactly where the responsibility does lie.
Let us realize when we are talking about this subject that we would have here not merely the 150,000 horsepower-part of which would be needed for the irrigation but a substantial part of which would be available for homes in the area and for agricultural machinery-but we would also have the core of a great grid system which could be multiplied several times. Each of us knows that if you have a sure source of constant power you can multiply that immensely by supplementary steam power or diesel power and still keep an economic level of power costs.

The time has come when the minister should clear the air. May I repeat that on June 10 last the minister had this to say:
We have been doing all right at clearing obstruction out of the way. There were four when we started discussions and there is now only the one left-the question of power development costs-
Mr. Speaker, as a member of this house from another part of Canada, and as one who believes this is not merely something of concern to Saskatchewan but something by which every Canadian wants to see Saskatchewan given the opportunity it should have to restore this great heartland to the province, I urge the government to act.
May I point out to hon. members opposite that a motion has been brought forward which gives them an opportunity to say to the government what they want done. If any member believes this project should proceed, then he has no right to vote against this amendment. If they believe it should be done, then let them vote for this amendment. I would suggest that the Minister of Agriculture, with the consent of the Prime Minister who sits beside him, might indicate something that can be done. That is that there be a free vote; that this be not regarded as a test of confidence, if that in any way could embarrass the government, but that he seek the support which he surely should ask in view of the unqualified promises he has made in the past. This would give everybody on his own side who wishes to see this project proceed a chance to vote without injury to his future relationship to the government.
We have been told by the Prime Minister on other occasions that ministers, and presumably members, can act according to their conscience. Let them act according to their conscience on this occasion. Let everybody here provide an encouraging and striking demonstration that there is no provincialism m this, but that members throughout this house from the Atlantic to the Pacific want something done in Saskatchewan which will be of immense value to that province and to the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not only to join with my colleagues in supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert, but also to support the appeal just made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that the government permit a free vote on this question.
I have been rereading Hansard this afternoon to confirm my memory on the point that two years ago we had an amendment
50433-241i
16, 1955	3819
South Saskatchewan River Project similar to this, moved by the same hon. gentleman who now represents the constituency of Prince Albert. That amendment was moved in February and was debated for several days, finally being voted upon on February 10, 1953, as recorded at pages 1813 and 1814 of Hansard.
During the discussion of that amendment which, though in slightly different language, was the same as the one now before us in that it called for the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project, one of the chief arguments put forward by the Minister of Agriculture and by others on the Liberal side of the house against voting for the amendment was that it was a motion of non-confidence. The Minister of Agriculture used almost the same language as he used this afternoon, when he looked in my direction and said I should know that an amendment of this kind is a motion of non-confidence, and that therefore those who support the government, have to vote against it.
Now, I am sure those who were here at that time will not ask me to read the record to substantiate what I am now saying took place in February of 1953, because the Minister of Agriculture, the Prime Minister1, and others who were here at that time will remember what happened then as well as I do. As I say, the result was that the amendment of the then member for Lake Centre, the present member for Prince Albert, was defeated. That, as I say, was on February 10, 1953, and is recorded in volume II of Hansard for that session.
I now turn to volume V of Hansard for that same session, and I would remind hon. members who were here that there was another motion to go into supply moved on May 6 of that year. On that occasion another member of the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), moved an amendment, one of those supposed amendments of non-confidence. Again it was moved as an amendment to the motion to go into supply. While on a different subject, procedurally it was exactly the same kind of amendment as the one moved in February concerning the dam.
Perhaps I should put the text of the second amendment on record so we will know what we are talking about. It is found at page 4850 of Hansard for May 6, and is as follows: That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
in view of the impending departure of the Prime Minister for Washington this house desires to record its opinion that further and more vigorous efforts should be made by the government to bring about the removal of the restrictions imposed by
3820	HOUSE OF COMMONS
South Saskatchewan River Project the United States on the importation of Canadian agricultural products, in violation of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
Following the speech of the hon. member for Eglinton there were speeches by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and then a speech by the Prime Minister. In the course of his speech the Prime Minister indicated that if it was understood that this amendment was not to be regarded as a motion of non-confidence in the government, he was willing that the house might pass the amendment, whereupon another motion could be moved to go into committee of supply and we could carry on with the day's business.
I am sure many of those present will recall that. But I ask the government and hon. members in the house generally to note that that happened in May, 1953, just a couple of months after we had been told by the Minister of Agriculture, "No, you cannot do that sort of thing". It looks as if it all depends upon the government's attitude toward the subject matter of the amendment. In the case of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton, apparently the government was not unwilling that the house should record itself in favour of the subject matter thereof; but in the case of the amendment moved in February, 1953, by the hon. member who is now the hon. member for Prince Albert, apparently the government felt differently.
So, Mr. Speaker, is it not pretty clear that what we are confronted with on these amendments to go into supply is not an ironclad and absolute rule that can be found somewhere in a book on procedure; rather that we are confronted with what the government tens us is the case each and every time. Sometimes the government says "This is a motion of non-confidence, and all Liberals must vote against it". And most Liberals, if not all, do vote against it. On the other hand, if the government decides it is a perfectly acceptable proposition and wants it to pass, then all Liberals vote for it, and it passes unanimously.
The occasion to which I refer, of May 6, 1953, is not the only one of recent date. I have here as well Hansard for 1951, and I would remind hon. members that on June 12 of that year there was an amendment to the motion to go into supply which, on that occasion, was moved by the Leader of the Opposition. Again the motion made by the government was a motion to go into supply. The amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition was, in the words of the Minister

of Agriculture today, and those of the hon. member for Rosthern, what is sometimes called a motion of non-confidence. According to them such a motion could not be carried without meaning the defeat of the government.
It so happens that on that occasion, as Your Honour will recall because of your interest in previous parliaments as well as in this one with respect to this matter, it dealt with a proposal to set up a special committee on procedure. That could lead into a discussion in which I shall not indulge at this time.
What was the attitude of the government on that occasion? Did the government say, "We will not let the Liberal party vote for this, because it would mean the defeat of the government"? No; the Prime Minister said that on the understanding that this was not to be regarded as a vote of nonconfidence, he had no objection to the acceptance of the amendment. Therefore on that occasion of June 12, 1951, the amendment to the motion to go into supply was adopted.
The government was not defeated, any more than it was on May 6, 1953. On each of those occasions, immediately after an opposition amendment to the motion to go into supply had been carried by the house -and in both cases this was done unanimously-a minister of the crown rose and moved again that the house do now go into committee of supply. I do not wish to endanger the chances of this procedure being followed again by emphasizing the fact that on at least one of those occasions the next motion to go into supply was subjected to an amendment as well, but that is just to make the record complete.
In addition to these two occasions I have mentioned, namely May 6, 1953, and June 12, 1951, there was the occasion on August 27, 1946, to which my colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie referred earlier, when there was before this house an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply. That amendment suggested that consideration should be given to the continuation of the milk subsidy.
After a number of hon. members had spoken, including a number of Liberal members who spoke in favour of the subject matter of the amendment, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) suggested that it might be regarded not as a vote of confidence or non-confidence in the government but that there should be a free vote. On that occasion, unlike the ones in 1951 and 1953 to which I have referred, there was a recorded vote, a division of the house. Even so, enough Liberals voted with those of us on

the opposition side of the house for the amendment to carry, but the government was not defeated and no election was brought on.
The reason nothing of that nature happened was that the government had said in advance it was not to be regarded as a vote of nonconfidence in the government. Accordingly, as soon as the milk subsidy amendment had been carried a minister of the crown moved that the house go into committee of supply. That second motion carried, we went into committee of supply and the business of the house went on.
I submit that the picture is becoming very clear as a result of these incidents. The hon. member for Rosthern made quite a speech this afternoon during which he gave us a few pointers on procedure and on the constitutional nature of our democracy. He made it clear that he felt it was his responsibility to try to keep the present government in office. The logical conclusion to be drawn from the position he takes, in the light of these various instances to which I have referred, is that when there is an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply, if the government says it is a motion of non-confidence and all Liberals must vote against it, they do vote against it; if the government says it is not a motion of non-confidence, that they like it, that they think it should pass, then Liberals vote for it; but if the government says it is not a motion of confidence or non-confidence, that they have no opinion, that they are prepared to let the members of the house have a free vote, then on an occasion such as that the hon. member for Rosthern and other Liberals vote as they feel they should on that particular issue.
I suggest that the picture has become somewhat confused, but at any rate surely this much is clear from what has come out of these debates on amendments to motions to go into committee of supply. We have had a clear indication as to where the government stands. Having been willing on some occasions to accept the opinion of the house, at least for its own guidance, and still feel it was not defeated; having been willing on other occasions to accept the subject matter of the amendment as satisfactory to the government, does it not follow that when the government says "No", when it says "This is a motion of non-confidence", when it says to the Liberal members of the house, "You must vote against it", that means the government is opposed to the subject matter of that amendment?
I suggest that if the government does not want to be left in the position of being unalterably opposed to proceeding with the
16, 1955	3821
South Saskatchewan River Project construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam and the irrigation project, it should on this occasion do as the Leader of the Opposition has suggested and permit a free vote of the members of this house.
We know where the Minister of Agriculture stands. As far as the project of the dam is concerned we know of all the documents he has pulled out of his pockets and the different statements he has made. But let it be said in all fairness to the minister that he is in favour of the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project. We know also from his forthright statements, both inside and outside the house, that the Prime Minister is not yet in favour of recommending to parliament the appropriation of the necessary money to go ahead with this project.
But what we do not know on any free basis is where all the hon. members of this house stand. We have had votes in the past that make it pretty clear that members of the opposition groups in this house favour proceeding with this project. But we do not really know where Liberal members stand. I suggest that it might be to the advantage of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture and other members of the government to find out where Liberal members stand. They will not find out simply by saying that this is a motion of non-confidence and therefore they must vote it down. If they will say, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said on August 27, 1946, that this is a free vote, or if they will accept it on the terms on which the Prime Minister accepted the motions in 1951 and 1953, we would have a chance to find out where the Liberal members of this house stand. I think that would be of value to the Prime Minister.
Of course if he wants to get advice from the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek who is trying to interrupt me, I am sure he is ready to give it to him at any time.
It is obvious from what I have been saying that I feel strongly about this project. I believe it is good for Canada as a whole. I feel that it should be proceeded with as soon as possible, but it is obvious that the hurdle we must get over first is the question of what the government is going to do. I suggest that the government would be well advised to find out where we all stand in this House of Commons, and the best way to do that is to permit a free vote on the amendment now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, since members from Saskatchewan who sit on this side of the house have been referred to on several occasions, I think I should take

South Saskatchewan River Project just a moment or two before the vote to state my position. There have been volumes of discussion on this topic. There have been royal commissions and investigations, and I think probably every angle of the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam has been thoroughly explored.
I stated my position last year, as can be found in Hansard, as being in favour of the project for three main reasons. First, as an irrigation project it would be an undertaking in the national interest. Second, as a power project it would justify itself. I emphasized last year that assuring as it would a constant water supply for the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina it would be a project of value, not only to Saskatchewan, but because these are two of the larger cities of Saskatchewan it would be in the national interest.
I indicated at that time that it would make a considerable change in the geography of Saskatchewan. After all, Saskatchewan is in Canada, and the project can be tied in for that reason. I pointed out that the construction of this dam would create a lake about two-thirds the size of lake Erie. To have such a body of water in the Palliser triangle would certainly, from every way you look at it, be in the national interest. I just want to restate those three points, without going into detail at this time.
There is no body of opinion in Saskatchewan opposed to the building of this dam. I remember well when the Prime Minister spoke in Regina during the last election. He dealt with this very question right in the heart of Saskatchewan, and he told us in his forthright manner that at this time the Saskatchewan dam would not be constructed. That is not saying no to the project, any more than it is saying no to a national health plan in Canada; but at the moment, in the judgment of the government, this does not seem to be the time to do it.
After all, this side of the house is responsible to the nation as a whole and must use its judgment in that way. Here perhaps I should not be too positive, because this is only my second year here; but it is all very well for the opposition to bring up resolutions or amendments that cover a very large field. As a matter of fact there is no limit to the field of resolutions that may be placed on the order paper by the opposition side. We on this side are saddled with the responsibility not only of promoting ideas, but this side of the house has the definite responsibility of doing the work. The opposition does the talking, but this part of the house does the work. It has the responsibility of finding the money for it.
You are not losing any weight.

I have the fullest confidence that the national business, which is the concern and responsibility of this government, is being conducted in a way that will redound to the national interest from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
I do not like to mention politics or political angles, but it has been stressed by several that in Saskatchewan this matter has been a political football. I want to tell this house that I have been in politics in Saskatchewan, if you wish to know, since 1925, when I attended my first nominating convention. That goes back quite a way. If anyone talks about playing political football, I think I know at least a little about it. I do not know what our C.C.F. friends in Saskatchewan would do with respect to digging up election issues if they did not have this issue to bring up.
If anyone in Saskatchewan has made the Saskatchewan dam a political football it has been our socialist friends in that province. Perhaps they would be in a sense economically happy, but I am telling this house they would be extremely unhappy if the Saskatchewan dam were built, because they bring that out from time to time and, along with the general socialist story of the broken promises the Liberal party has been strewing throughout Saskatchewan, this is always one of the promises that is dragged out of the basket at election time. If anyone has made this issue a political football, it is our socialist friends in the province of Saskatchewan, and everyone in Saskatchewan knows that.
I am not afraid. I have no hesitation in voting against this amendment, because most of the people in my area, and I believe most of the people in Saskatchewan, are beginning to see the political angle of this issue and who are using it as a political football. If I cast my vote, and I am recorded in Hansard as voting against the amendment, I can project myself two or three years hence, should I again be a candidate. I can see someone planted in the back of the hall when I happen to be getting right down to the core of things with regard to the splendid record of this government; I can see him pop up and say, "What about the Saskatchewan dam?"
That has been played over and over again, and they are not going to get by with it this time; that is certain. I have no qualms of conscience whatsoever in casting my vote as a vote of confidence in favour of the government. I am not going to vote against the construction of the dam, but I am going to vote against this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, at the risk of being caught in a nutcracker, the Saskatchewan members on

opposite sides of the house, I am going to say a few words on this subject. I have listened to discussion of the Saskatchewan dam in this house for a long time. As I understand it, at the present time practically everyone in Saskatchewan, including the Minister of Agriculture, wants to build that dam. The drawback seems to have been that the Prime Minister is still doubtful whether the project is in the national interest. I assume he is wondering whether he can justify such an expenditure by the federal government in one province for the purpose for which it is intended. I am going to try to help him out a little.
We have already had an expression of opinion from Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. I am going to say something now on behalf of the province from which I come. I think he is quite justified in concluding at this time that he is quite safe in making the expenditure, on the grounds he himself sets out, but he is afraid he may be accused in other parts of Canada of subsidizing power in the province of Saskatchewan. Now, he can disabuse his mind of that charge, because he is on safe ground when he is able to tell the rest of the people of Canada that Saskatchewan has a legitimate reason to ask the federal government to make an expenditure of some $62 million in that province, even if it is to some extent going to help the development of power. In the development of the St. Lawrence seaway, as far as the province of Ontario is concerned, one of the greatest advantages this province is going to get is the power development at Niagara falls. So indirectly the province of Ontario is going to be heavily subsidized in the provision of power for the future through the St. Lawrence seaway. The people of Saskatchewan are going to pay their proportionate share in helping to develop that power as a sideline of the St. Lawrence seaway project.
If anyone is still doubtful on that point all he has to do is say we have been looking at the future of power in Canada, and we have decided that not far away is the possibility of atomic energy; so in searching around for a place to set up a pilot plant, which is going to cost the federal government some money, we have decided that we are going to establish in this province of Ontario an atomic energy reactor in co-operation with the province, in order that we may be in that field of power in the future. So we are assisting the province of Ontario on two counts in the development of power.
On that score the Prime Minister is legitimately entitled now, after canvassing the situation for a long time, to say to his supporters that the time has come for the people
South Saskatchewan River Project of Canada as a whole to look upon this project in Saskatchewan as a national project.
In the second place, in view of the fact that, according to what I heard this afternoon in debate, the province is prepared to spend some $78 million in this development, the federal government's share to be about $62 million, I think the province is carrying a fair share. We are going to develop Canada for the future. As we build up our country through immigration and other means I hope we are not going to confine our thinking just to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and consider them as the great centres, with the rest of the country as the hewers of wood and drawers of water. I assume that we are going to do something to expand the economy in every province so we may be able to accommodate more people.
From listening to discussions of the matter and reading something about it, I understand that with the development of power through this project there is a possibility of getting some kind of a diversified economy. At the present time it is a wheat economy, a one-crop economy. This economy is subject to the whims of the elements. If it could be diversified by some industrial expansion on the prairies, through this power development, the chances are that over the long pull it may be possible to save in wheat subsidies more than the amount of money that is being asked should be put into this particular project. In any case, I think members in all parts of the house should take the question out of the realm of politics.
Someone mentioned the Canso causeway. We know that matter was the subject of long argument; 10 years, in fact. We had a commission on it. However, it was not until we sold the people in our end of the country on the idea that this was not a political issue, formed a committee in that province representative of all parties, and took the project completely out of the realm of politics, that we got some sanity into the thinking of all concerned. Everybody wanted it but nobody wanted the other fellow to get any advantage from it. Once we neutralized the question we went ahead and got something done.
I think that is the attitude that must be taken with respect to this project. I do not think there is anyone in the maritime provinces, at least, who would object to the federal government throwing in the amount of money that is asked here. We realize that Saskatchewan is in much the same position as the maritime provinces. There are many things they would like to do. There are many things they know should be done. If they had the finances with which to do it provincially they would undertake this project
South Saskatchewan River Project themselves. But they have not the finances provincially, and I think they are legitimately entitled to ask the rest of Canada to throw in something in order to help them do something that, in my opinion, will mean a great deal to that province in the future.

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?
Question.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a grievance at this time. My grievance is that there is a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on the question of capital punishment whose report has not yet been made; and at 12.05 tonight Pacific time, or 3.05 a.m. our time, a young man will be hanged in Vancouver. I maintain he should not be hanged.
I raise this grievance as a matter of emergency because this is the only opportunity I shall have to save a man's life. I want to say this, sir, that in accordance with all the rules and the laws of parliament the matter has gone through the courts and has been considered by the cabinet.
I may say, sir, that I submitted a presentation to the only one who has the power to receive or consider any presentation on behalf of this man, Robert Alexander Hoodley. May I just read a part of my communication, because it states the grievance rather briefly. It is, as I have said, an emergency grievance because this man is to hang tonight, and only this parliament can save his life.

I appreciate your remarks very much, Mr. Speaker. I think you understand that I am not discussing anything which has to do with the prerogative of a general expression of mercy, but this grievance deals with only one case. As you have said I may proceed, I should like to do so because it must be done tonight. I am raising this question in order to ask the members of the House of Commons to request the cabinet to exercise their prerogative of mercy and revise a decision they have made. I refer to the case of Robert Alexander Hoodley, who has been sentenced to hang tonight.
Since my time is short I am going to present the case very briefly. This young man, Robert Alexander Hoodley, was born in Shanghai in December, 1934, and because of an unfortunate family situation developed a serious abnormal behaviourism. The experience of going through the war years as a very young child also had a detrimental effect. I believe his record amply demonstrates a very unstable nature, and discloses that he was subject to violent and inexplicable reactions.
Administration of Justice
He was examined by Dr. R. A. E. Richmond of the child guidance clinic in 1950 and found to be in a mental condition. Since the date of the homicide he has been examined by Dr. Richmond and Dr. Whitman, who are both very highly regarded psychiatrists, and I am given to understand that he has been classified as an aggressive psychopath, and in the opinion of the examining doctors is given to violent, impulsive behaviour that can explode almost spontaneously because he appears to be motivated by a hairtrigger stimulus.
The person killed by Mr. Hoodley was the stepfather of his fiancee. It is a matter of record that Miss Patricia Walsh, the fiancee, told Mr. Hoodley that her stepfather had forced sexual relations upon her. This being the case, I think it can be understood why on the spur of the moment young Hoodley took the impulsive action which resulted in the committing of homicide. One cannot condone this young man's action, and without any question of doubt he must be placed in an institution where society would be protected from his impulsive neuroticism.
However, in view of all the circumstances I do feel that the death penalty, which is mandatory by law, should be commuted by the governor general in council to a term of life imprisonment. This matter went before the cabinet last Friday. Because I understand I cannot be given information before it becomes public, I was not notified until 2.45 this afternoon-though I asked for the information last Saturday-that the cabinet had turned down this plea for clemency.
In view of the fact there is now a committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on capital punishment; in view of the fact it is hoped by the joint chairmen of the committee and all the members that we can have a report on capital punishment this session; in view of the fact that here we have a case where all the evidence shows that the man is an aggressive neurotic and that he shot his fiancee's stepfather because of the rape of his fiancee, I say there is only one power now that can save this boy's life and put him under guard in an institution, and that is this House of Commons. I recognize that the House of Commons can only advise the Prime Minister and the cabinet. The House of Commons can only ask the Prime Minister and the cabinet to meet-to meet tonight-and give at least a stay of execution, but with the hope of commutation of sentence to life imprisonment.
Sir, it is not very often I ask anything of this nature, but I feel strongly about it. I wish to thank the Prime Minister for having

Administration oj Justice given me the opportunity to speak to him today. I know I am not alone in thinking as I do. Other members of all parties feel the same way, and have spoken to the Prime Minister.
Sir, because it is now approaching ten o'clock, and because I do not want this application wiped out by Your Honour calling it ten o'clock, I shall conclude by asking the House of Commons-the only group who can now do it-to request the Prime Minister and the cabinet to meet tonight and commute this sentence which, if they do not intervene, will be fulfilled by a boy being hanged, a boy who is neurotic, aggressive, hairtrigger, and who shot a man because his fiancee was raped by her stepfather. If they do not intervene the sentence will be carried out at 3.05 E.D.T.
Sir, I thank you for the opportunity given to me to speak on this matter. I shall not move any amendment, but shall rest in the hope that the House of Commons will express its opinion that this sentence should not be carried out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a discussion of this kind is quite irregular, and has been refused by Mr. Speaker at Westminster on more than one occasion. I appreciate the hon. member's intense feeling about this matter, but I can assure him that he is misinformed about certain of the facts, or certain of the things he has mentioned as facts in connection with this case.
The case was very carefully considered by those who had the constitutional responsibility to consider it, and it is not a responsibility that anyone enjoys having to exercise. It was very carefully considered on two occasions. On the first occasion it was considered because the time at which it had to be considered had arrived, and a conclusion was reached after a very serious study of the record of the facts that were proved, and that

are not in accord with the information the hon. member has and in which I am sure the hon. member honestly believes.
The facts that were before us were the facts that had been proved before the court. There are very eminent psychologists who believe that our law is not as it should be, but we have to apply it as it exists. There was a serious and honest endeavour to reach a proper conclusion. A recommendation for His Excellency was prepared and was signed; but before it reached His Excellency news arrived that a court in British Columbia had granted a reprieve to allow special application to be made for an appeal to the supreme court. That application was made, for special leave to appeal to the supreme court. It was denied.
After it was denied the case was reconsidered, and we had all the facts before us. The hon. member, in his approach to me, told me quite frankly that he had no new facts, but felt that we had not made a proper appreciation of those that were before us. Well, we had the constitutional responsibility of making that appreciation and to us it appeared, as it appeared to the jury and to the court of appeal, to be a cold-blooded murder, committed under circumstances which, in accordance with practice that has been followed in recommendations to the crown, would not justify a recommendation for interference with the course of the law.
We had to come to that conclusion, and we came to that conclusion. There has never been any occasion when there was an attempt by any House of Commons, either here or in the United Kingdom, to go behind the exercise of that terrible responsibility we have to discharge.
On motion of Mr. Argue the debate was adjourned.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, May 17, 1955
